value.reason: lib/insecurity.ts:41 defines `hash` as plain, unsalted MD5 (`crypto.createHash('md5')...digest('hex')`). The data flow shows this same function protects stored credentials: the password setter in models/user.ts:70-75 calls `this.setDataValue('password', security.hash(clearTextPassword))`, and passwords reach it through the registration path (register form → POST /api/Users → the finale-generated model write). Part of the login query in routes/login.ts:34 is redacted, but the remaining text (`... AND «SECRET»')}' AND deletedAt IS NULL`) has the shape of a `«SECRET»')}'` comparison, so login checks credentials against the same MD5 digest. This matches the positive example (MD5 used for password storage and comparison) and not the negative one (MD5 used only for an ETag). MD5 is fast and unsalted, so these password hashes are cheap to crack, which is CWE-916. That also falls short of the appropriate security safeguards for authentication secrets that DPDP Rule 6(1)/6(1)(a) requires. The SQL injection on the same line is a separate issue and doesn't change this verdict.
